name: Job

overview.author: Unknown. Suggestions include Job himself, Moses, Solomon, or an unnamed wise man. The book is anonymous.
overview.date: The events seem to take place in the patriarchal era (Job offers sacrifices as head of his family and measures wealth in livestock). The date of writing is uncertain, anywhere from Solomon’s time to the exile.
overview.audience: God’s people of every age who wrestle with suffering, justice, and the ways of God.
overview.setting: The land of Uz, probably east of Israel near Edom, along with scenes in the heavenly court.
overview.purpose: To explore why the righteous suffer, to reject the simple idea that suffering always means punishment, and to show that God’s wisdom and sovereignty are worthy of trust even when His reasons are hidden.
overview.structure: A prose prologue (1–2), poetic dialogues between Job and his three friends (3–31), Elihu’s speeches (32–37), God’s speeches from the whirlwind (38–41), and a prose epilogue (42).

outline.title: Job’s Lament and the First Cycle of Speeches

items.title: Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar, and Job’s replies
God disciplines and teaches through suffering

themes.title: The Mystery of Suffering
themes.text: Job’s suffering is not punishment for sin. The reader knows what Job does not: his faith is being tested.

themes.title: Wrong Answers
themes.text: Job’s friends insist suffering always means sin. God says they have not spoken rightly (42:7).

themes.title: Honest Lament
themes.text: Job pours out complaints and questions to God, yet never curses Him.

themes.title: God’s Sovereignty and Wisdom
themes.text: God answers not with explanations but by revealing His majesty as Creator.

themes.title: Faith Without Reasons
themes.text: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (13:15). Job’s faith is purified through suffering.

themes.title: The Need for a Mediator
themes.text: Job longs for an arbiter, a witness, a Redeemer between him and God (9:33; 16:19; 19:25).

christInBook.text: Job longs for an arbiter who could lay his hand on both God and man; Jesus is that one Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).
Job’s living Redeemer who will stand on the earth points to the risen Christ.
Job, a righteous sufferer accused by Satan, foreshadows Jesus, the truly innocent sufferer.
Job prays for the friends who wronged him, as Christ intercedes for us (Luke 23:34).

crossReferences.note: The steadfastness of Job and the Lord’s compassion.
The depth of God’s wisdom (quotes Job 41:11).
Wrestling with the prosperity of the wicked.
Light momentary affliction and eternal glory.

reflection: Job worshiped God after losing everything (1:20–21). How do you respond to God when you lose something precious?
Job’s friends were right to sit silently for seven days and wrong when they began to explain. How can you comfort a suffering friend well?
Job brought his raw complaints to God instead of walking away. What honest lament do you need to bring to God?
God answered Job with Himself, not explanations. Can you trust God without knowing the reasons?
Job “saw” God in a new way through suffering (42:5). How has God revealed Himself to you through a hard season?

chapterList.title: Job’s Losses
chapterList.summary: Job, a blameless and upright man in Uz, is greatly blessed. In the heavenly court Satan claims Job only fears God because of His blessings. God permits Satan to test him. In one day Job loses his oxen, donkeys, sheep, camels, servants, and all ten children. Job tears his robe, worships, and says, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.”
questions: What is Satan’s accusation (1:9–11)?
What limits does God place on Satan?
What do you learn from Job’s response (1:20–22)?

chapterList.title: Job’s Illness and His Friends
chapterList.summary: Satan says a man will give anything for his life. God permits him to strike Job’s body, but not take his life, and Job is covered with painful sores. His wife says, “Curse God and die.” Job answers, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” His three friends come and sit with him silently for seven days.
questions: How does Job’s answer to his wife show his faith (2:10)?
What did Job’s friends do well at first (2:11–13)?
How can your presence comfort someone who is suffering?

chapterList.title: Job Curses His Birth
chapterList.summary: Job breaks the silence by cursing the day he was born and wishing he had died at birth. He longs for the rest of the grave and asks why life is given to those in misery.
questions: How does Job’s lament compare with his earlier response?
Is it sinful to express such deep despair to God? (See Jeremiah 20:14–18.)
What do you do with feelings of despair?

chapterList.title: Eliphaz’s First Speech
chapterList.summary: Eliphaz gently reminds Job that he has encouraged others. Then he states his principle: the innocent do not perish, and those who plow iniquity reap trouble. He describes a mysterious night vision questioning whether any man can be righteous before God.
questions: What is Eliphaz’s main assumption (4:7–8)?
What truth and error are mixed in his words?
How can true principles be misapplied to someone’s suffering?

chapterList.title: Eliphaz Urges Job to Seek God
chapterList.summary: Eliphaz says man is born to trouble and urges Job to seek God and commit his cause to Him. He says Job should not despise God’s discipline and promises restoration if he repents.
questions: Which of Eliphaz’s statements are true in general (5:17–18)?
Why are his words still misguided for Job’s situation?
How does Paul quote Eliphaz (1 Corinthians 3:19)?

chapterList.title: Job Replies to Eliphaz
chapterList.summary: Job says his anguish is heavier than the sand of the sea and that God’s arrows are in him. He wishes God would crush him. He accuses his friends of being like a dried-up stream, offering no help when he needs it.
questions: How does Job describe his friends (6:15–21)?
What does a suffering person need from friends (6:14)?
How can we be dependable friends in hard times?

chapterList.title: Job Complains to God
chapterList.summary: Job describes life as hard service with months of emptiness and nights of misery. He turns to speak directly to God, asking why God watches him so closely and won’t leave him alone.
questions: How does Job’s view of life reflect his pain (7:1–6)?
How does Job’s question in 7:17–18 twist Psalm 8:4?
What is it like to feel God’s attention as a burden rather than a blessing?

chapterList.title: Bildad’s First Speech
chapterList.summary: Bildad bluntly says God does not pervert justice; Job’s children must have sinned. If Job is pure, God will restore him. He appeals to the wisdom of past generations: those who forget God wither like papyrus without water.
questions: How does Bildad’s view of Job’s children wound him?
What is right and wrong about appealing to tradition (8:8–10)?
Why can rigid theology lack compassion?

chapterList.title: Job: How Can a Man Be Right Before God?
chapterList.summary: Job agrees that God is just and powerful, but asks, “How can a man be in the right before God?” God is so great that no one can argue with Him. Job longs for an arbiter who could lay his hand on them both.
questions: What does Job affirm about God’s power (9:4–10)?
Why does Job feel hopeless about arguing with God?
How does Jesus fulfill Job’s longing for an arbiter (9:33)?

chapterList.title: Job’s Plea to God
chapterList.summary: Job speaks in the bitterness of his soul, asking God why He contends with him when God’s own hands formed him. He asks to be shown his sin and to have a little comfort before he dies.
questions: How does Job describe God’s care in forming him (10:8–12)?
Why does that make his suffering more confusing?
Have you ever asked God, “Why?” What did you learn?

chapterList.title: Zophar’s First Speech
chapterList.summary: Zophar rebukes Job’s many words and says that God has exacted less than Job’s guilt deserves. He speaks of God’s unsearchable wisdom and urges Job to put away iniquity so his life will be brighter than noonday.
questions: What is harsh about Zophar’s claim in 11:6?
What truth does Zophar express in 11:7–9?
How can true theology be cruelly applied?

chapterList.title: Job: God’s Wisdom and Power
chapterList.summary: Job sarcastically answers that his friends think wisdom will die with them. He affirms that God controls all things, including nature and nations, and that wisdom and might belong to Him, but this does not explain his suffering.
questions: How does Job affirm God’s sovereignty (12:10, 13)?
Why does Job’s knowledge of God not solve his problem?
How do you hold God’s sovereignty and your pain together?

chapterList.title: Job Wants to Argue with God
chapterList.summary: Job says his friends are “worthless physicians” who should be silent. He wants to argue his case with God directly: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him.” He asks God to show him his sins.
questions: What does 13:15 reveal about Job’s faith?
How were the friends “whitewashing with lies” (13:4)?
Why does Job believe his honesty is better than their defense of God?

chapterList.title: Life Is Short
chapterList.summary: Job reflects that man is born of woman, few of days, and full of trouble. A tree may sprout again, but a man dies. “If a man dies, shall he live again?” He longs for God to hide him until His anger passes.
questions: How does Job describe the brevity of life?
What hope does Job reach toward in 14:14–15?
How does Jesus answer Job’s question about resurrection (John 11:25)?

chapterList.title: Eliphaz’s Second Speech
chapterList.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of undermining the fear of God with his words. He describes the terrors that come on the wicked man, implying Job is such a person.
questions: How has Eliphaz’s tone changed since chapter 4?
What is Eliphaz implying about Job?
How can frustration make us less compassionate?

chapterList.title: Job: Miserable Comforters
chapterList.summary: Job calls his friends “miserable comforters.” He describes God as an enemy who tore him in anger. Yet he declares, “Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven.”
questions: What would Job do differently if they were in his place (16:4–5)?
How does Job describe God’s attack?
Who is Job’s witness in heaven (16:19)? How does this point to Christ?

chapterList.title: Job’s Spirit Is Broken
chapterList.summary: Job says his spirit is broken and his days extinct. He has become a byword, and his hope seems buried with him in the grave.
questions: How does Job feel about his reputation?
Where does Job place his hope (17:15–16)?
How can you encourage someone who feels hopeless?

chapterList.title: Bildad’s Second Speech
chapterList.summary: Bildad describes the fate of the wicked: their light goes out, they are trapped, terrors frighten them, and their memory perishes. He clearly assumes Job is wicked.
questions: How does Bildad paint the fate of the wicked?
Why is this speech especially painful for Job, who has lost his children?
What is the danger of assuming we know why someone suffers?

chapterList.title: I Know My Redeemer Lives
chapterList.summary: Job laments that God has wronged him, his family has abandoned him, and even his breath is strange to his wife. Then he rises to astonishing hope: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth... in my flesh I shall see God.”
questions: How does Job describe his isolation (19:13–19)?
What does Job confidently hope for (19:25–27)?
How is Jesus our living Redeemer?

chapterList.title: Zophar’s Second Speech
chapterList.summary: Zophar insists that the joy of the wicked is short. They may enjoy evil like a sweet morsel, but God will make them vomit up their riches. He describes the heavy judgment that awaits.
questions: What is true about Zophar’s description of the wicked?
Why does it not apply to Job?
How does Psalm 73 deal with the prosperity of the wicked?

chapterList.title: Job: The Wicked Often Prosper
chapterList.summary: Job challenges his friends with reality: the wicked often live long, prosper, and die in peace, while others die in bitterness. Their tidy theory does not match experience.
questions: What evidence does Job give that the wicked prosper?
How does this challenge the friends’ theology?
How should God’s people handle the apparent injustice of life?

chapterList.title: Eliphaz Accuses Job of Great Sins
chapterList.summary: Eliphaz now directly accuses Job of specific sins: exploiting the poor, withholding water from the weary, and sending widows away empty. He urges Job to return to God and receive his treasure in Him.
questions: What sins does Eliphaz invent?
What true invitation does Eliphaz give (22:21–23)?
How should we respond when falsely accused?

chapterList.title: Job Longs to Find God
chapterList.summary: Job wishes he knew where to find God so he could present his case. He searches forward, backward, left, and right, and cannot find Him. Yet he says, “He knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold.”
questions: What does Job long for (23:3–5)?
How does 23:10 express faith in God’s purposes?
How does suffering refine faith like gold (1 Peter 1:6–7)?

chapterList.title: Why Doesn’t God Judge?
chapterList.summary: Job asks why God does not set times for judgment. He describes the oppression of the poor and the crimes of the wicked that seem to go unpunished.
questions: What injustices does Job describe?
How do you deal with the question “Why does God allow this?”
How does 2 Peter 3:9 shed light on God’s timing?

chapterList.title: Bildad’s Third Speech
chapterList.summary: Bildad briefly declares God’s great dominion and asks how man, a maggot and a worm, can be righteous before Him.
questions: What is true in Bildad’s statement about humanity?
Why does this short speech suggest the friends have run out of arguments?
How does the gospel answer Bildad’s question?

chapterList.title: Job: The Fringes of God’s Ways
chapterList.summary: Job mocks Bildad’s unhelpful counsel, then describes God’s power over the deep, the heavens, and the sea. These are “but the outskirts of his ways,” and we hear only a whisper of Him.
questions: How does Job describe God’s power in creation?
What does “the outskirts of his ways” (26:14) suggest about our knowledge of God?
How should God’s vastness affect your prayer life?

chapterList.title: Job Maintains His Integrity
chapterList.summary: Job swears he will hold fast to his righteousness and not lie. He describes the end of the wicked, agreeing that ultimately God judges them.
questions: Why does Job refuse to admit sins he did not commit?
What is the difference between integrity and self-righteousness?
How does Job agree with the friends here (27:13–23)?

chapterList.title: Where Is Wisdom Found?
chapterList.summary: A poem describes how people mine the earth for silver, gold, and gems, yet wisdom cannot be found or bought. Only God knows its place. “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.”
questions: How does the poem compare searching for wisdom to mining?
Why can’t wisdom be bought?
How does 28:28 summarize biblical wisdom?

chapterList.title: Job Remembers Better Days
chapterList.summary: Job remembers when God’s friendship was on his tent, his children were around him, and he was respected. He helped the poor, the fatherless, the widow, and the blind, and he was “eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.”
questions: What made Job’s past life so good?
How did Job use his position to help others?
How do you handle memories of better seasons?

chapterList.title: Job’s Present Humiliation
chapterList.summary: Now younger men mock him, his health is ruined, and God seems to have cast him into the mire. “I cry to you for help and you do not answer me.”
questions: How has Job’s status reversed?
How do you think Job feels about God’s silence?
How does Jesus enter into this kind of suffering (Isaiah 53:3)?

chapterList.title: Job’s Final Defense
chapterList.summary: Job makes a solemn oath of innocence, listing sins he has avoided: lust, deceit, adultery, mistreating servants, neglecting the poor, trusting in gold, idolatry, and gloating. He signs his defense and demands God answer him.
questions: What does Job’s covenant with his eyes (31:1) teach about purity?
How does Job connect the dignity of servants to God (31:13–15)?
Which of these standards challenges you most?

chapterList.title: Elihu Speaks
chapterList.summary: Young Elihu, angry at Job for justifying himself rather than God and at the friends for finding no answer, speaks up. He has waited because of his youth, but “it is the spirit in man... that makes him understand.”
questions: Why is Elihu angry with both Job and the friends?
What does 32:8–9 say about the source of wisdom?
How can younger believers speak with both boldness and humility?

chapterList.title: Elihu: God Speaks Through Suffering
chapterList.summary: Elihu says that God speaks in dreams and through pain to turn people from pride and keep them from the pit. A mediator may show a person what is right, and God says, “Deliver him... I have found a ransom.”
questions: How does Elihu see suffering as God’s warning or teaching?
What does 33:23–24 suggest about a mediator and ransom?
How has God used pain to speak to you?

chapterList.title: Elihu Defends God’s Justice
chapterList.summary: Elihu insists that God cannot do wickedness or pervert justice. God sees all a person’s ways, and Job has added rebellion to his sin by speaking against God.
questions: What does Elihu affirm about God’s character (34:10–12)?
Is Elihu fair to Job?
Why is it important to affirm God’s justice even when life feels unjust?

chapterList.title: Elihu: God Is Not Affected by Us
chapterList.summary: Elihu argues that our sin or righteousness does not harm or benefit God. People cry out under oppression but do not seek God their Maker, “who gives songs in the night.”
questions: What does Elihu mean that God gives “songs in the night” (35:10)?
Why might prayers that ignore God Himself go unanswered?
What songs has God given you in dark times?

chapterList.title: Elihu: God Disciplines to Deliver
chapterList.summary: Elihu says God does not despise anyone. He opens people’s ears through affliction. Elihu begins praising God’s greatness in the storm: “Behold, God is great, and we know him not.”
questions: How does Elihu describe God’s purpose in affliction (36:15)?
How does Elihu’s speech prepare for God’s appearance?
How can you see God’s greatness in nature?

chapterList.title: Elihu: God’s Majesty in the Storm
chapterList.summary: Elihu describes thunder, lightning, snow, and wind as God’s works, and asks Job to consider God’s wondrous works. “Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed with awesome majesty.”
questions: How does Elihu use weather to show God’s power?
How does 37:23–24 summarize Elihu’s message?
When did nature last cause you to worship God?

chapterList.title: The LORD Answers from the Whirlwind
chapterList.summary: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?” He questions Job about creation, the sea, the dawn, light, snow, the stars, and the rain.
questions: Why does God answer with questions rather than explanations?
What does God reveal about Himself through creation?
How do God’s questions put your problems in perspective?

chapterList.title: God’s Wisdom in the Animal World
chapterList.summary: God continues questioning Job about wild animals: lions, ravens, mountain goats, wild donkeys, the wild ox, the ostrich, the horse, and the hawk. God cares for creatures that humans never see.
questions: What does God’s care for wild animals reveal?
How does Jesus use similar examples (Matthew 6:26)?
What does this teach about God’s attention to details?

chapterList.title: Job Humbled; Behemoth
chapterList.summary: God challenges Job, “Will you even put me in the wrong?” Job answers, “I am of small account... I lay my hand on my mouth.” God continues, inviting Job to consider Behemoth, a mighty creature only God can master.
questions: How does Job’s response change (40:3–5)?
What does God’s question in 40:8 reveal about Job’s error?
Why does God point to powerful creatures?

chapterList.title: Leviathan
chapterList.summary: God describes Leviathan, a terrifying sea creature no human can tame. “Who then is he who can stand before me? ... Whatever is under the whole heaven is mine.”
questions: If no one can stand before Leviathan, what does that say about standing before God?
What does 41:11 teach about God’s ownership?
How does Paul quote this in Romans 11:35?

chapterList.title: Job Repents and Is Restored
chapterList.summary: Job confesses that God can do all things and that he spoke of things too wonderful for him: “Now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes.” God rebukes the friends for not speaking rightly as Job did, and Job prays for them. God restores Job’s fortunes double, and he has seven sons and three daughters.
questions: What has changed in Job (42:5–6)?
Why does God say Job spoke rightly and the friends did not?
What does Job’s prayer for his friends teach about forgiveness?

tagline: Suffering, God’s wisdom, and faith that holds on
readingPlan: 42 chapters: one chapter a day takes 42 days; two a day takes about 21 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
